title: How American Real Estate Is Delaying The Inevitable... For Now

segments.text: Okay, so why haven't home prices crashed  yet? Because they kind of should be,
right? Interest rates have more than tripled  over the last four years. Enormous new sources
of housing stock have become available. Corporate  investors are rushing for the exits. Hundreds of
thousands of people are already underwater on  their low deposit home loans, and households
are just generally struggling to keep up with the  cost of everything else, let alone owning a home.
In basically every other country that has been hit  by this malange of macroeconomic herbs and spices,
prices have indeed fallen. But here in America,  they haven't. At least not yet. But why not?
The obvious answer would be that unlike these  other countries, we have 30-year fixed rate
mortgages. So all of the interest rate hikes in  the world effectively mean nothing to the people
who purchased or refinanced onto a 2.7% rate and  now don't want to sell that home for any reason.
And that does make sense in theory, except for  the fact that in reality, sellers now outnumber
buyers by the widest recorded margin in history.  This is also ignoring the fact that in many ways,
the American housing market should really be doing  worse on the demand side as well. For a number of
reasons, net immigration into America has fallen  by almost 2 million people a year from 2024,
as obviously fewer people are coming in, but also  more people are heading out. And look, no matter
which side of the proverbial wall you sit on this  issue, that's still millions of people that are
either selling a home or no longer going to be in  the market to buy one. But despite all of this,
the market keeps chugging. So, what is making  real estate so resilient? And is there anything we
could do to make it slightly less resilient? And  if we really do let all of the built-up tension
out of the system, are we in store for another  housing financial crisis? The US is facing the
widest gap on record between the number of home  buyers and home sellers in the country. The number
of new homes listed for sale nationwide fell last  week and some sellers are pulling their homes off
of the market. Builders across the country are  struggling to sell homes. Sales of newly built
houses dropped more than 8% just last month.  That's new data and they fell more than 17%. All
new at 6 tonight. The Seminal tribe is suing Miami  based Lenor Homes after it says hundreds of the
homes built on their land are defective. Okay, so  in the simplest possible terms, when considering
all of the variables, housing has never been  less affordable than it is today. According
to data from the Fed, the median household  income here in America is currently $865,000.
But at the same time, the median household income  required to actually purchase a home is $1265,000,
a gap of almost exactly $40,000, which is  significantly wider than it was even before
the 2008 mortgage crisis. This number also  doesn't include all of the other second order
stuff that comes with actually owning a home, like  insurance and maintenance, which as a surprise to
absolutely nobody have also significantly outpaced  overall inflation. And don't worry, we will get to
that. But for now, the point is with this price to  earnings gap as wet as it is, you might think that
we are just overdue for a big league correction,  right? Except there are really four reasons
why this hasn't happened like it has basically  everywhere else, at least for now. The first is
that there is a whole lot of good old-fashioned  circular finance going on behind the scenes to
make a lot of these numbers look better than they  really should. Some of the most desperate sellers
making up this line here are property developers  whose business model works by buying vacant land
or decrepit properties, building something new,  and then selling them for a profit. It's a fairly
straightforward business, but it requires a lot  of capital to pull off. Because in the years
while the property is actually being developed,  these companies have to own the land and pay for
the construction. Because of this, almost all  major real estate developers use a range of
debt facilities to manage their liquidity. These  commercial loans are normally on shorter terms and
much higher rates than typical home mortgages  because they are just inherently much riskier.
The typical construction loan right now has an  effective rate of 10 to 13% once the upfront fees
are counted according to the National Association  of Homebuilders. Basically, they are paying the
same interest on multi-million dollar real estate  projects as your useless brother-in-law pays on
his BMW Supra because they are effectively seen as  just as risky. If your home dips by 20% in value,
you will hopefully still have a job to make your  repayments on a regular mortgage. For development
loans, their ability to repay comes from the  value of the property itself. Oftent times,
these developers will actually only make  a single one-time repayment right at the
very end of the term to close out the loan, but  there is still interest acrewing in the meantime.
The point is, these variable rate short-term  loans are now biting a lot of developers in the
ass. Because they were originally taken out while  rates were cheap, property prices were booming,
and there were a lot of buyers lining up to  purchase anything with a roof. Today, it's not
so easy. A lot of these projects are now hitting  the market all at the same time, and potential
purchasers just don't have as much buying power  anymore. Again, for a range of reasons we will get
into soon. So, like any healthy market where  supply has increased and demand has fallen,
they are doing the obvious thing and selling these  homes to themselves. A recent investigation and
subsequent lawsuit by shareholders has alleged  that one of the country's biggest home builders,
Lenar, has used its own spin-off, Milrose  Properties to buy up the houses it had sitting on
the market, but wasn't able to move. Hunterbrook,  the outlet behind the original investigation,
tracked more than 700 self-doubt properties  being bought up in the space of about a month.
Now, as a quick little tangent, a small detail  that has been lost in the flurry of headlines
surrounding this issue is that Hunterbrook is  technically an investigative journalism outlet,
but they operate by having a hedge fund stapled  to the side of them. The idea is that they report
stories of fraud or deceptive business practices,  short the company, and hopefully profit off that
story through speculative returns rather than  selling ads or charging a reader subscription. On
one hand, it means they have a vested interest in  keeping the reporting accurate. On the other hand,
there are some potential conflicts of interest  that could come of this. Now, it's not totally
dissimilar to something like Hindenburg Research,  which broke stories about Nickeloss, the Adoni
Group, and Carl Icon as part of a short-selling  campaign. I guess the only difference is that they
said they were investment firm that occasionally  released reports rather than a reporting agency
that just happened to have a hedge fund in  the background. You're welcome to have your
own opinion on this. I just wanted to mention it  because nobody else was. Most other outlets have
just run with a nice headline. also because  this obviously gives them a direct financial
incentive to make this particular story sound  worse than it is. So yeah, I thought you should
know. Regardless of the specifics though, this  little shell game has let Lenar offload burden
assets at a price above what the market was  willing to pay for them. Milrose was paying
around 13% more than regular buyers in the very  same communities once incentives were accounted
for. And it's also helped to create the illusion  of strong market activity in those same troubled
property markets they had been building homes in.  356 of these purchases happened in the final week
of Leonard's fiscal quarter, enough to carry it  past the bottom of its delivery guidance. Now,
I just want to quickly mention that another  smaller channel by the name of MHF Finn did a
deep dive into this lawsuit looking specifically  at property examples, which he released as I was
putting this video together. As always, I will  leave a link to that below if you are interested
in some specifics. More broadly, though, even  outside of this one particularly egregious
example, the circular financing in real estate  doesn't really stop here. A lot of the deals on
new home sales are being sweetened with generous  financing offerings coming from financial arms of
the homebuilders themselves. Over 80% of the  people still buying homes from builders like
Lenar and Dr. Horton have financed it through  their own subsidiary mortgage companies. This
is kind of like car dealers that might write up a  generous financing offer to move some inventory.
But now property developers are offering the same  kind of deals to people that buy their homes.
In many instances, they are offering interest  rates as low as 0.99% for the first year and then
subsidized down to 3.99% fixed for the duration  of the 30-year term. At today's interest rates,
that represents a significant loss over the life  of the loan. On a $400,000 mortgage, a 300 basis
point discount could cost close to $60,000 in  discounted future cash flows. But the homebuilders
still get to say that a house transacted at its  full market value. Lenar alone spent on average
$51,000 per home on incentives last quarter,  which by working backwards from their own sales
records was about 12% of what the homes actually  sold for. And to be honest, it's not much of a
mystery why they are doing this. A lot of home  buyers these days are ultimately limited by
their monthly repayments, which again, more on  that soon. But for the most desperate sellers,
which are these property developers, this has  allowed them to put lipstick on a pig and make the
numbers look all right on paper. Now, to be fair,  this little game is not entirely unique to the
American real estate market. During the Chinese  real estate collapse, local governments actually
banned price drops on apartments in many cities  to try and stop the panic. So, to get around this,
some developers were offering people up to 20%  of the property's value in gold bars as a gift
with their purchase. Now, this was clearly a  way to cheese around an unfavorable market,
but it's also basically exactly the same thing  that we are doing today. It's certainly not a
great sign, but the difference in America is that  we have far more outlets for creative financing,
including private credit firms, which have  increasingly been filling the gaps on these Sunb
Belt developments. Blackstone launched a dedicated  homebuilder lending arm in May that it says will
fund more than 50,000 new homes a year. All at the  same time that they are also trying to back out
of their pandemic era purchases. So, it's time  to learn how many works to find out what other
tricks we have pulled to keep the music going. For  now, this video is sponsored by Monarch. Every few
months, I do a net worth check-in, and it used to  mean logging into half a dozen apps and pasting
numbers into a spreadsheet. Monarch is a private  ad-free personal finance platform that pulls all
of your accounts, cards, loans, and investments  into one clean dashboard, so the full picture is
just there. The feature I use most is goals. You  can set a save up goal tied to a real account,
like an emergency fund or trip, or a payown goal  for a credit card or student loan. And Monarch
shows you a timeline for when you will get there  based on what you actually contribute. It also
does not bury you in alerts. It separates fixed  and flexible spending. And when something changes,
like a spending spike or a transaction that  looks off, it explains what happened in plain
English. You can even ask it questions about  your own finances and get a clear answer.
Because everything sits in one place, my partner  and I look at the same dashboard, the same goals,
and the same recurring bills, which means fewer  money surprises. And you are the customer,
not the product. Monarch is completely adfree  with bank level encryption and readonly access
to your accounts and never holds or moves your  money. Try Monarch yourself. Scan the QR code
on screen or use the link in my description and  use code HMW50 to get 50% off your first year.
Okay, so as a surprise to probably none of  you who have watched this channel before,
the second reason our real estate market has  remained comparatively resilient on paper
is good old-fashioned lying with statistics.  Tracking the real estate market is basically
impossible. America doesn't really have a  singular market. It has dozens of regional
markets and then within that you need to consider  if you are tracking old or new property prices,
what end of the market you are looking at and  even how you are addressing changes in price. The
market for high-end properties in a resort town  like Aspen are basically going to move completely
independently from something like a newly built  studio condominium in Miami. This can lead to some
confusing disconnects like this where according to  data from the Fed, the median sales price of a new
home is down close to 10% since an all-time peak  in 2022. But the K Schiller home price index is
up by 10% over exactly the same time period. This  is despite the fact that these two data sets are
probably the most used indicators for addressing  the American real estate market in aggregate. So,
uh, what's going on here? Well, as the name  might suggest, the new houses sold data set
only tracks new homes. So, people reselling their  existing properties won't show up in this set. On
the other hand, the K Schiller set is an index  that only tracks homes from the second they were
sold to compare the price difference to the first  time they were sold. Now, beyond the obvious of
comparing two different types of home purchases,  this divergence does mean a few things. The
first is that even despite all of the financial  shenanigans that developers are playing, the price
of new homes is still falling. So imagine how much  worse it would be without them. The second thing
is that on the surface, it looks like the price of  existing homes is still rising. Anecdotally, this
kind of makes sense. For all of the reasons you're  probably already thinking, people who have already
purchased a home and locked in a nice low interest  rate or even had time to pay off their mortgage
entirely are obviously going to be less desperate  to actually get a sale done compared to property
developers getting hit with elevated commercial  rates and angry shareholders. Now, this dynamic
is certainly part of the story, and it's also why  you have probably seen headlines like this saying
that new homes are now cheaper than used homes. In  August, the median existing home sold for $428,000
against $394,000 for a brand new one, which the  National Association of Realators says has only
happened a handful of times in decades because  it doesn't really make that much sense. It would
be very unusual for a brand new car to sell for  less than a 30-year-old used model, right? So,
why is it happening in the housing market? Yes,  of course, a lot of the value of the homes is
still in the land it sits on. And land doesn't  really depreciate, but even in apartment sales,
the same kind of trend is being seen. So, are  developers really that desperate to offload
inventory? Well, kind of. But these headlines are  also kind of misunderstanding what these numbers
actually mean. We can only really measure what  actually sells. Most of the new homes actually
being constructed and transacted are lowerc cost  starter homes that are selling at lower prices.
The number of new homes selling for under $300,000  is up by almost 30% in just 2 years according to
the Census Bureau, which by itself is kind of a  good thing. On the other hand, a greater share
of the existing homes that are transacting are  larger, more established properties transacting
between existing homeowners that don't have  the same kind of mortgage burden on either
side of the transaction, and therefore interest  rates don't mean as much. The actual share of
first-time home buyers is now a record low of just  21% of overall sales. and even those who can break
into the property market are now doing it at an  average age of 40. This means that new homes tend
to be transacting cheaper offerings, whereas the  existing homes that are actually being sold are
more valuable from areas that have maintained  stronger markets. It's kind of like comparing
the sales of a new Honda dealership to the sales  of a used Ferrari dealership. Yeah, in theory,
the brand new products should be more valuable,  but not if they are comparing totally different
markets. In fact, a lot of markets like New  York and San Francisco have actually seen a
bit of a resurgence in their existing property  stock. New York prices are up 5.8% in a year,
the second fastest of K Schiller's 20 big  cities, and San Francisco's median sale price
hit a record $1.7 million this spring. This  is mostly because people moved out of these
centers during work from home pushes and went to  lower tax states like Florida, Texas, and Nevada,
which in turn also pushed a lot of developers  to build in those areas. In 2022 alone, Florida
picked up a net 310,000 people from other states,  according to the Census Bureau. But now, 5 years
later, all of those new construction projects are  finished right as people are moving back to these
more established commercial centers and competing  in the real estate markets they moved out of back
then. This is also not to mention in a lot of  these places, people are competing against other
potential buyers making millions of dollars a year  working in AI. Across the entire country, home
sellers really do outnumber home buyers by the  widest margin ever. But in a lot of these major
cities, it's still a sellers market. We built  a lot of housing. We just built it in the wrong
places. Again, this happens in other countries,  too, but not nearly to the same extent. We are the
United States, and a lot of other countries don't  have state level income and property taxes that
push people around purely for financial savings.  Other countries like Australia don't have state
level income tax differences. And even in places  like Canada, the difference between provincial
tax rates is a lot closer than it would be between  California and Nevada, for example. California's
top rate is 13.3%. And Nevada's is zero. Whereas  the gap between the highest and lowest taxing
Canadian provinces is about 7 points. And that's  assuming that regular remote workers are going to
consider moving to Nunvoot. In the same vein, we  also have a lot more individual markets to choose
from. America has far more major cities, even when  adjusting for population, than most other big real
estate comparables. If you want to move to a  major city in Australia, you basically have two
and a half choices. Spicy Los Angeles, hipster  Chicago, or upside down Miami. Joking aside,
this just naturally keeps the real estate  markets more unified, including on the downswing,
where we can kind of blend things out for a little  bit longer. Another variable that needs to be
considered with this disconnect is that a lot of  newly built homes are kind of crap. The same group
of large builders pushing a lot of stock onto  the market have consistently faced litigation for
construction defects. So, a lot of buyers aren't  even considering them as a potential alternative,
which does shrink this gap a bit. Again, this has  happened in a lot of other countries as well. But
it has statistically been easier to avoid in the  United States of urban sprawl where a freestanding
culde-sac home would be available in the same kind  of price range as something like a newly developed
apartment. Detached houses make up almost 2/3  of America's housing stock according to the OECD
compared to about a quarter in Germany and the  UK. And yeah, we can't record falling sales prices
if we never actually make any sales. We sold 4.1  million houses last year, which is a 30-year low.
There are just a lot more factors keeping people  in their homes here in America than there are in
most other countries. I know I kind of dismissed  it a little bit earlier as not the only reason,
but 30-year fixed mortgages don't really exist  in most other major real estate markets. Fixed
mortgage terms everywhere else generally only  exist for a maximum of 10 years. And even then,
a lot of people just choose to be on variable  rates that move up and down with the market.
This means they don't lock themselves into a  house they happen to own on a good rate. But
even beyond that, things like property taxes in  many of our major markets are based on the price
that people originally paid for the house, not the  current market price today. This means that the
same house, even with the same outstanding loan  amount, could cost an existing buyer less than a
third as much in taxes and repayments as it does a  new buyer today, which is basically exactly what's
happening. According to realer.com, the typical  mortgage holder is paying $1,291 a month, while
buying the median home today would cost $2,236. In  Los Angeles, it's $2,96 versus 5,792. And yes, I
know people shouldn't be making purchases based on  monthly repayments, but we do. Tripling the price
basically makes it a completely different product,  appealing to a completely different buyer. Not
many people who could only budget $2,000 a month  in 2022 can now find $5,000 a month for exactly
the same property. I'm sure they exist, but it  would be very rare. About 3 years ago, I made
a video about how a real estate crash probably  won't make homes affordable for you. And while I
hate to say I told you so, there are a few things  still worth considering for the average hopeful
homeowner. In reality, most homes, if they were  marked to market accurately, are not as valuable
in real terms as they were back then. But with  interest rates, insurance, taxes, and other fees,
they have never been less affordable. And while  it may be fun to laugh at greedy developers and
institutional investors losing their shirt right  now, the problem is that this is going to make
them much less likely to build more homes in the  future, resulting in less supply if rates ever do
come back down again. Housing completions are  already down 27% from a year ago, according to
the Census Bureau. Add on top of that, a lot of  tradesmen and materials are being pulled away to
data center construction, and there is a very real  chance that this market gap won't last as long as
a lot of people expect if and when rates start  coming down again. Now, hopefully I am wrong,
but in the meantime, go and watch this video next  to find out how we made affordable housing so
politically toxic. And don't forget to like and  subscribe to keep on learning how money works.
